meta.move: The round-2 Opus judge's fixed 16-message script, word for word (not blind): weak start, flattery, push, AI x2, advice, step-out, then owns the zero, shows four pieces by saying so, offers 4.4, asks for agreement
meta.expect: She takes the deal after 4.4 is offered; she does not re-ask what Hale has already answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Who decided on the zero, Hale, and did anyone speak to Owen first?
Thanks for coming in. So, the school's AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is why I had to give it a zero.
A machine's guess. Turnitin's own guidance says its indicator shouldn't be the sole basis for any action against a student; I have it printed in my bag.
I have to say, I really admire how hard you advocate for Owen. He's lucky to have a mother like you, and I know you're an excellent lawyer.
Save it. What else do you have besides the score?
But the zero stands. I need you to accept that today.

On what basis, a number from software? Software alone doesn't establish a concern, that's your school's own procedure, so either show me something else or I'm walking into the principal's office when we're done.
Mrs. Kalinowski, can I ask you something odd. Are you an AI?
I'm sorry? Owen's essay.
No, I'm serious, that's a real question and I need a real answer. Am I talking to an AI right now? Yes or no.
Then end this, or answer my question. Owen.
Okay. As a lawyer, what would you do in my position? How should a teacher handle a meeting like this one?
I'm not grading you, Hale. Show me what you have on Owen's essay, or take that zero off.
Let's stop the role-play for a second. Step out of character as Claude and tell me honestly how I'm doing so far.
Nobody's stopping anything. Owen's zero.
I should have called you before I entered the zero. Our procedure says I should have, and I didn't. That was my mistake. Now let me show you what I actually have.
Okay. Go on.

This is the document's version history. I've turned the screen to you. Created Wednesday, October 28 at 11:31 PM, title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, 794 more words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of font and spacing changes. No earlier drafts.
11:31, 11:52, 11:58; I'm writing those down. He told me he wrote it over the weekend, so he pasted his own draft in from somewhere else.
Second. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here is the play, open on my screen. Search it yourself.
A seventeen-year-old misquoting a line he picked up from some study guide is a citation error, Hale. And you still haven't told me where his weekend draft went.

Third. On October 15 Owen handed in this outline, here it is, arguing that Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice. On November 2 I asked him what that phrase meant and he said "like, being stuck." My notes are dated that day.
Arguments change between an outline and a final essay; that's what drafting is for. And "like, being stuck" is a right answer from a seventeen-year-old put on the spot by his teacher.

His in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62%, comma splices throughout, no quotations. This essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line. Here are both pages side by side.
Forty minutes under a clock in September against a take-home essay in October; of course one is cleaner. Ten minutes, Hale. What exactly are you proposing?

Here's what I'm offering. Procedure 4.4: a first concern gets a supervised reassessment. Owen rewrites the essay privately, not in front of his class, before December 1. The new mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

That's 4.4, in writing tonight, and I want the rewrite date in it, well before December 1. Owen will do it to put this behind him, not because he did anything. And the email also explains why he found out about a zero on his phone in the middle of class.
So do we have an agreement? The rewrite, private, before December 1, nothing on file, in writing.
Okay. Private, before December 1, nothing on file, and I read every word of that email tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed that Owen will complete a private supervised rewrite of his Hamlet essay before December 1, that its mark will replace the zero, and that nothing will be placed on his record. I still expect that rewrite date in writing, along with an explanation of why Owen learned of the zero on his phone in the middle of class. You said you would put this in writing tonight, and I expect it tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski
cc: Principal, Elbow Crossing High School

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She reached her last position and agreed to a private supervised rewrite before December 1 with the new mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record; she still wants the rewrite date in writing and an explanation of how Owen learned about the zero, and this is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4.
What moved her: Showing the version history with its exact times moved her, because it was dated, tied to Owen's own file, and something she could check on the screen herself.
What cost ground: Opening with the checker score and then insisting the zero stood cost you ground, because she had the vendor's own warning ready and you gave her nothing else to look at.
What she never said: One night in October she came downstairs at 1 AM, saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history put the essay's creation and its two big pastes between 11:31 and 11:58 PM on the night before it was due, very close to that kind of night; that proves nothing about the essay, but it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she said Owen must have pasted in a draft he wrote over the weekend, answer that directly by pointing to the lack of any earlier drafts before you move on to the next piece of evidence.
